items.text: Last time, we scored the model's mistakes: the lower the score, the better.
We scored every setting of the two knobs and drew the scores as a landscape. The lowest point is the best setting.
With two knobs, that's easy.
But a big model can have hundreds of billions of knobs, way too many to map.
So the model's like someone blindfolded on a mountain, with no idea where the valley is.
How does it find the bottom?
It uses something called gradient descent. Let's see how it works.
So picture yourself up there, trying to reach the valley.
You can't see, but your feet feel which way the ground tilts, and how steeply.
So you feel for the steepest way down, and take one small step.
Feel again, step again, and you get there.
For the model, the slope underfoot is how much the score changes when you nudge each knob a little.
Put those slopes together, and that's the gradient. It shows every knob the fastest way down.
Gradient descent turns all the knobs one small step that way, then checks the slope again.
The learning rate sets the step size, and you pick it before training starts.
Let's try it on the taxi map: base fare across, per-kilometer rate up.
Darker means a higher score. The fares are made up.
We start at a five dollar base fare and two dollars a kilometer: a score of seventy-eight, way up high.
First, feel the slope: nudge each knob up ten cents.
Raise the base fare, and the score drops one point seven. Raise the per-kilometer rate, and it drops eleven point two.
So turn both up, but the per-kilometer slope is much steeper.
Our first step turns that knob the most.
In three steps, the score falls from seventy-eight to twenty-five, twelve, nine, and we're in the valley.
The floor is a long, gentle trench.
The base fare creeps up, the per-kilometer rate eases back, and we inch along.
Gentler slopes mean smaller steps, so we slow down.
After a thousand-odd steps, the score is about two. The true minimum is one point nine seven.
The knobs end up near a ten-dollar base fare and two fifty a kilometer.
It never saw the whole map. It only felt the ground underfoot.
That run used a learning rate of zero point zero zero five. What if we'd picked wrong?
Here are three paths from the same start, same number of steps.
Make it ten times smaller, and it heads the right way but crawls.
It ends at a score of five point five, still far from the bottom.
Make it about four times the original, and it overshoots across the valley, ending higher than where it started.
Then it climbs higher and higher, past a hundred.
Five steps in, it's off the map.
Our original rate walks steadily to the bottom.
That's why the learning rate is often the single most important setting in training.
Too big, and it bounces right off the map. Too small, and you waste time.
Big models use gradient descent too, with two upgrades.
First, there's too much data to read it all every step.
So each step grabs a small random batch, roughly estimates the slope, and goes. That's stochastic gradient descent.
The path wobbles, but it saves loads of computing and still ends up near the bottom.
GPT-3, for example, saw only about one part in a hundred thousand of its training data per step.
Second, the steps get smarter. A method called Adam gives each knob its own step size, based on its past slopes.
GPT three was trained with Adam, and Meta's Llama uses a tweaked version.
That's how GPT-3's one hundred seventy-five billion knobs got turned, one small step at a time.
Gradient descent is walking downhill blindfolded: feel for the steepest way down, and take a small step.
And the learning rate sets the size of each step.
But a model with just two knobs can only learn so much.
Next time, we'll stack lots of little units in layers, each with its own knobs, and see what happens.
That's called a neural network.
